## Why this comparison

`VisCollin` [@viscollin] is the reference R implementation of the
Belsley-Kuh-Welsch collinearity diagnostics [@belsley1980] and of their
graphical display (tableplots and collinearity biplots) proposed by Friendly
and Kwan [-@friendly2009]. It works on `lm` and `glm` objects, so it is the
natural point of comparison for `multiCollglm`. This article answers three
questions on real data:

1. What exactly does `VisCollin::colldiag()` compute when it is given a
   **GLM**?
2. Does `multiCollglm` reproduce it, and with which setting?
3. Where do the two give different answers, and why?

The short answers are: `colldiag()` decomposes the **original design matrix**
and ignores the family, the link and the IRLS weights, which is exactly
`multiCollglm`'s `method = "X"`; the two coincide to machine precision
there; and they differ whenever the information matrix $X'\hat W X$ is not
proportional to $X'X$, which is the usual case in a GLM.

```{r}
library(multiCollglm)
library(VisCollin)

# TEMP of the Lee data is stored on a /100 scale; multiply it back by 100
lee <- LeeCancer
lee$x6100 <- lee$x6 * 100

mods <- list(
  Lee      = glm(y ~ x1 + x4 + x6100, family = binomial(), data = lee),
  Nitrogen = glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = Gamma(link = "inverse"),
                 data = Nitrogen),
  Mine     = glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = poisson(), data = Mine),
  Plastic  = glm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4, family = poisson(), data = Plastic)
)
```

## What `colldiag()` does with a GLM

The relevant lines of `colldiag()` are (VisCollin 0.1.4):

```r
X <- mod$model[, -1]                 # drop the response from the model frame
X <- na.omit(X)
if (add.intercept) X <- cbind(1, X)  # default: FALSE
X <- scale(X, scale = scale, center = center)
svdX <- svd(X)
```

So, for a `glm`, it takes the columns of the **model frame**, optionally adds
a column of ones, scales them (by default, dividing each column by its
root-mean-square, without centering) and takes the SVD. The fitted model
itself is never used: no family, no link, no IRLS weights. Its defaults
(`add.intercept = FALSE`) reproduce SAS `PROC REG ... COLLINNOINT`, following
the argument of Fox [-@fox1997] that diagnostics including the intercept
are only meaningful when it has a real interpretation.

Dividing by the root-mean-square instead of by the Euclidean norm multiplies
every column by the same constant, $\sqrt{n-1}$, so condition indices and
variance proportions are the same as with unit-length columns.

## Where they coincide: `method = "X"`

With `add.intercept = TRUE`, `colldiag()` and `bkw_diagnostics(method = "X")`
decompose the same matrix, $X_{ul}'X_{ul}$ (original design matrix, unit
length, intercept included, no weights). For the four datasets of the
package:

```{r}
same <- sapply(mods, function(m) {
  cd <- colldiag(m, add.intercept = TRUE)
  bk <- bkw_diagnostics(m, method = "X")
  c(
    max_diff_condition_index = max(abs(cd$condindx[, 1] - bk$condition_index)),
    # colldiag() stores components in rows; multiCollglm in columns
    max_diff_proportions     = max(abs(t(cd$pi) - bk$proportions))
  )
})
t(same)
```

The differences are floating-point noise: condition indices and proportions
agree to at least ten significant digits. The same holds for
the `colldiag()` default (no intercept) when the GLM is fitted without
intercept:

```{r}
m_noint <- update(mods$Mine, . ~ . - 1)
c(colldiag    = max(colldiag(m_noint)$condindx),
  multiCollglm = condition_number(m_noint, method = "X")$condition_index)
```

Hence the one-line translation table:

| `VisCollin` | `multiCollglm` |
|:---|:---|
| `colldiag(mod, add.intercept = TRUE)` | `bkw_diagnostics(mod, method = "X")` |
| `colldiag(mod)` (no intercept, the default) | `bkw_diagnostics(<mod fitted without intercept>, method = "X")` |
| `colldiag(mod, center = TRUE)` | not available (centering is deliberately not offered) |
| largest condition index | `condition_number(mod, method = "X")$condition_index` |

## Where they differ (1): the IRLS weights

In a GLM the precision of $\hat\beta$ is governed by the information matrix
$X'\hat W X$, not by $X'X$. When the weights $\hat W$ are not constant,
the collinearity of the *regressors* (what `colldiag()` measures) and the
conditioning of the *information matrix* (what the default
`method = "WS"` measures) are different things. For the same models:

```{r}
cn <- function(m) {
  c(`VisCollin (colldiag)` = max(colldiag(m, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
    sapply(c(WS = "WS", MP = "MP", X = "X", RAW = "RAW"),
           function(k) condition_number(m, method = k)$condition_index))
}
knitr::kable(t(sapply(mods, cn)), digits = 4,
             caption = "sqrt(CN) on the same data; the VisCollin column equals method X.")
```

For these four applications the weighted definitions are **larger** than
the unweighted one (Lee: 190.78 with `colldiag()`, 315.14 with `"WS"`;
Plastic: 595.74 against 876.84), so a diagnostic that ignores the weights
understates the ill-conditioning of the estimation problem. In other
applications the difference may go the other way, or vanish; what matters
is that it cannot be known without computing the weighted version.

The same happens with the variance-decomposition proportions. For the Lee
model both approaches single out the intercept and `TEMP` (`x6100`) in the
largest dimension, but with the weights a third dimension becomes
problematic as well (`sqrt(CN)` 31.96, against 11.80 with `colldiag()`),
and the proportions of the other dimensions are distributed differently:

```{r}
print(colldiag(mods$Lee, add.intercept = TRUE), fuzz = 0.3)
bkw <- bkw_diagnostics(mods$Lee)            # method = "WS"
bkw
```

### When the weights are constant everything coincides

If $\hat W$ is a multiple of the identity, weighting does nothing and the
three scaled definitions collapse into the one of `colldiag()`. That is the
case for a Gaussian model with identity link (the linear model):

```{r}
m_gauss <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = gaussian(), data = Mine)
c(colldiag = max(colldiag(m_gauss, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
  sapply(c("WS", "MP", "X"),
         function(k) condition_number(m_gauss, method = k)$condition_index))
```

and, less obviously, for a Gamma model with log link, whose IRLS weights are
identically 1 (see the [Bodyfat
article](reproduction-bodyfat.html)):

```{r, eval = have_vc && requireNamespace("TH.data", quietly = TRUE)}
data("bodyfat", package = "TH.data")
m_body <- glm(DEXfat ~ age + waistcirc + hipcirc + elbowbreadth + kneebreadth +
                anthro3a + anthro3b + anthro3c + anthro4,
              family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = bodyfat)
range(m_body$weights)
c(colldiag = max(colldiag(m_body, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
  sapply(c("WS", "MP", "X"),
         function(k) condition_number(m_body, method = k)$condition_index))
```

## Where they differ (2): the model frame

Because `colldiag()` reads `mod$model[, -1]`, what it analyses is whatever
sits in the model frame, not the design matrix the model was fitted with.
Two consequences, both easy to hit in a GLM:

**Prior weights and offsets are treated as regressors.** A model fitted with
`weights =` (very common for binomial or Poisson-rate models) stores the
weights in the model frame as a column called `(weights)`, which then enters
the diagnostic as if it were an explanatory variable:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
d <- Mine
d$w <- runif(nrow(d), 1, 3)
m_w <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = poisson(), data = d, weights = w)

colnames(colldiag(m_w, add.intercept = TRUE)$pi)   # VisCollin
rownames(bkw_diagnostics(m_w, method = "X")$proportions)  # multiCollglm
```

**Factors are not expanded.** `multiCollglm` works on
`model.matrix(mod)` (dummy variables, interactions, polynomial terms
included), whereas `colldiag()` receives the raw factor:

```{r}
d$f <- factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), length.out = nrow(d)))
m_f <- glm(y ~ x1 + f, family = poisson(), data = d)

res <- try(colldiag(m_f, add.intercept = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
cat(if (inherits(res, "try-error")) res else "no error")
rownames(bkw_diagnostics(m_f, method = "X")$proportions)
```

(With `colldiag()` the usual work-around is to pass `model.matrix(mod)[, -1]`
as a matrix instead of the model.)

## Where they differ (3): visualization

`VisCollin` has what `multiCollglm` does not: the **tableplot** and the
**collinearity biplot** of Friendly and Kwan [-@friendly2009]. `multiCollglm`
returns tables only. The two are not exclusive: the tableplot only needs a
list with the condition indices and the proportions, so it can be drawn from
a GLM-aware decomposition by wrapping it in a `colldiag` object:

```{r}
as_colldiag <- function(bkw) {
  ci <- matrix(bkw$condition_index, ncol = 1,
               dimnames = list(seq_along(bkw$condition_index), "cond.index"))
  structure(list(condindx = ci, pi = t(bkw$proportions)), class = "colldiag")
}
```

```{r tableplots, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "49%", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5}
tableplot(colldiag(mods$Mine, add.intercept = TRUE),
          title = "VisCollin::colldiag (original X)")
tableplot(as_colldiag(bkw_diagnostics(mods$Mine)),
          title = "multiCollglm, method = \"WS\"")
```

Left: collinearity of the regressors. Right: conditioning of the
information matrix of the Poisson model. In the Mine model both point to the
intercept and `x2` in the last dimension, but the weighted version
reaches a larger condition index (28.6 against 19.9).

*A caveat on the tool itself:* in the version used here (0.1.4),
`tableplot()` fails with an error when a variance proportion rounds to 100
(for instance with the Lee data), because of how the colour classes are
cut; this is why the Mine data are used for the plots.

## Summary

| | `VisCollin` | `multiCollglm` |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Model classes | `lm`, `glm` (as a model frame), matrices | `glm`, `glmnet`, `cv.glmnet` |
| Uses family, link and IRLS weights | No | Yes (`"WS"`, `"MP"`, `"RAW"`); no with `"X"` |
| Original design matrix, unit length | Yes (`scale = TRUE`) | `method = "X"` |
| Intercept | Excluded by default (`add.intercept`) | Always included (detects non-essential collinearity) |
| Centering | `center = TRUE` | Not offered |
| Design matrix | model frame (factors, `(weights)`, offsets not handled) | `model.matrix()` |
| Condition index and BKW proportions | Yes | Yes (same numbers for `method = "X"`) |
| RVIF [@salmeron2025] and ML-collinearity [@lesaffre1993] | No | Yes |
| Regularized fits (`glmnet`) | No | Yes (refit on the active set) |
| Tableplot and collinearity biplot | Yes | No (tableplot can be drawn from `bkw_diagnostics()`, see above) |

In practice: for a **linear model**, or to look at the collinearity among the
regressors themselves, `VisCollin` and `multiCollglm(method = "X")` are
interchangeable, and `VisCollin` adds the graphics. For a **GLM**, the
default `method = "WS"` is the diagnostic of the matrix that actually
determines the precision of the estimates.

## Reproducibility

The comparison was run with the code of `VisCollin` 0.1.4 (GitHub
version); the version installed when this page is built is shown below.
The only functions of `VisCollin` used are `colldiag()` and `tableplot()`.
